Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

courses.description: This course is a study of Modern American history from the end of WWII to the present day. The course will focus on military conflicts, Civil Rights, equality, political issues as well as technology and inventions since World War II. An emphasis will be placed on the United States' role in the world as a result of these topics as well as counterculture that develops. This course will use literature, music and film to interpret the importance of our most recent history. This class will require reading, writing and class participation! This course will fulfill the high school requirement for US History.
courses.fulfills_text: This course will fulfill the high school requirement for US History.
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Upon teacher and guidance counselor recommendation, a student can be placed in a foundational skills section within this class. Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

courses.description: There are many ways to learn about our nation's history. History is more than just dates and wars. This course examines US History, beginning with the Westward Expansion era to contemporary times, through a multimedia approach. We will learn our nation's history by examining photographs, newspaper articles, political cartoons, and other publications. We will also listen to and put into historical context music and film from different historical eras. Through this multimedia approach, we will learn about our nation's struggles and successes. We will examine equality and civil rights for all Americans, social and racial injustices, advancements in technology, politics at the national and international level, and American democracy. This course will fulfill the high school requirement for US History.
courses.fulfills_text: This course will fulfill the high school requirement for US History.
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Upon teacher and guidance counselor recommendation, a student can be placed in a foundational skills section within this class. Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

courses.description: History is a story; a story that is uniquely experienced by each individual. Civics is how an individual conducts themself and participates in local, state and national activities as a citizen of a nation. This course examines US History from a civic perspective. We will examine what it means to be a citizen. We will look at the rebellion of colonists and the revolution that led to the creation of The United States of America and its experiment in democracy. This course will introduce students to the workings of the American Government at the local, state and federal levels as well as introduce students to national historical documents like the Declaration of Independence, The US Constitution, and the Bill of Rights. We will discuss the role of an individual in society, their community, and the impact an individual can have on society. We will learn our nation's history by examining an array of historical documents and texts, first person accounts, and primary sources. We will learn about our nation's struggles and successes. We will examine equality and civil rights for all Americans, social and racial injustices, advancements in technology, politics at the national and international level, the idea of American democracy, and the stories of individual citizens who lived during the different time periods we study.
courses.fulfills_text: Catalog: "All students in Grade 10 or Grade 11 are required to take either U. S. History or Scholars of U. S. History (Advanced)." (US History credit required for graduation)
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Upon teacher and guidance counselor recommendation, a student can be placed in a foundational skills section within this class. Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

courses.course_code: 0122 (Scholars of US History 1 (A)) / 0123 (Scholars of US History 2 (A))
courses.description: Designed for the advanced student, this course will survey the entire history of the United States in great depth. Students must have above average skills in reading and writing as the pace will be accelerated.
courses.fulfills_text: All students in Grade 10 or Grade 11 are required to take either U. S. History or Scholars of U. S. History (Advanced).
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Full Year.

courses.description: This course involves a survey of the history and culture of the Western World from the Mediterranean civilizations to the Renaissance. This course will provide the student with information that will be needed in many college level social science courses. This is a higher level course, requiring average to above average skills in reading comprehension and writing. This course is a must for students considering any of the Social Sciences in college (i.e. Anthropology, Sociology, History, Political Science, Archeology). This course will emphasize research, writing, presenting and collaboration with peers.
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall.

courses.description: This course concentrates on Western Europe's modern political, social, and economic development. This course will span from the Protestant Reformation to present day Europe. This is a higher-level course, requiring average to above average skills in reading comprehension and writing. This course is a must for students considering any of the Social Sciences in college (i.e. Anthropology, Sociology, History, Political Science, Archeology). This course will emphasize research, writing, presenting and collaboration with peers.
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Spring.

courses.description: This course will study, analyze and debate the topics of; functions of government, school culture, substance abuse, mental health, teen violence and delinquency, race and gender issues, relationships, hate crimes, legal issues related to technology, current events, and topics that students choose to explore. Students will have the opportunity to present topics that they feel are current social issues. Students will be required to research various issues, work independently and in groups, and participate in class discussions. This course will introduce students to social issues that are currently affecting Americans in various parts of the nation, as well as internationally. The course succeeds when students share and substantiate their opinions, as well as participate in discussion.
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

courses.description: Virtues, ethics, values, fairness, right, and wrong. What exactly is justice? This class aims to explore that question by combining elements of civics, law, criminal justice, and philosophy in the pursuit of an understanding of justice in America. We will consider many questions including: what rights do people have? How should criminals be punished? What makes a law just? Is everyone treated fairly in the United States? Students should be prepared for a lot of reading, writing, and class discussion, as well as interactive activities such as a mock trial.
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

courses.description: This course focuses on how money, markets, and decisions actually work in the real world, and how economic thinking helps explain those outcomes. Students begin with core economic concepts such as incentives, supply and demand, and how markets function, then spend much of the semester developing and running a real business using start-up funds, creating products or services, and working with real customers. Alongside the business project, students learn practical personal finance skills and knowledge they will use after high school, including an understanding of housing and mortgages, investing and retirement, credit and debt, taxes and paychecks, and how marketing and advertising influence people’s decisions when buying and selling. The course also includes career readiness work such as creating a professional resume, practicing job interviews, and reflecting on how economic and financial choices shape outcomes over time. This class is best suited for students who enjoy hands-on projects and want to understand how real-world decisions add up over time.
courses.prerequisites: 1 US History credit or Scholars of US History (A)
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

courses.description: This course will study the history of genocide from the early 1930's to present day. It will include an extensive study of the Holocaust and its causes as well as post WWII genocides including: Cambodia, Bosnia, Rwanda and Sudan. This course will look at discrimination and intolerance and how it fuels hatred and the destruction of groups of people. This course emphasizes critical thinking, analytical reading, writing, group discussion and self reflection.
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

courses.description: This course is an introduction into the field of Psychology. We will study the history of Psychology, Psychologists of the 18th-21st centuries, human development, human behaviors, and mental functioning, examine psychological disorders, and Psychology in the 21st century. Throughout the semester we will be examining many aspects in the field of Psychology. We will be looking at the definition of Psychology, the brain and how it functions (or does not function), human and animal behavior, some very influential people who have contributed to the field of Psychology, motivation and emotions, intelligence and different states of consciousness. We will also study specific mental disorders, medications used to treat disorders, how psychological illnesses affect individuals and their relationships, and what YOU can do with or for someone who is suffering from a psychological disorder. This course is designed to be college-like in rigor, independence, and responsibility. Students must complete their work thoroughly and timely. There is an expectation that students will be completing work outside of the classroom, and/or preparing papers and projects for completion.
courses.prerequisites: 2 Social Studies credits (One of which must be taken at the advanced level)
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

courses.description: Turn your ideas into reality. By using the 3D modeling CAD(computer aided design) software SketchUp, learn to create both assigned and original designs. Once your design is complete, learn how to take that design and convert into a 3D printed model using plugins and a 3D printer. Following your design from model to print will allow you to go through real-world problem solving and optimization applications in order to see your vision become a reality.
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

courses.description: Taking the skills mastered in 3D Modeling & Printing Technologies, using SketchUp and slicing software learn to take your 3D designs to the next level. Learn how to reverse engineer items and take them from finished products to 3D designs then redesign them to make something new or better. The primary focus of this course will be to complete high quality 3D prints for use or for prototyping and create tutorials for future use. You will also learn how to take your SketchUp model and send those designs to our laser cutter or CNC router to turn your prototype into a usable product.
courses.prerequisites: 3D Modeling & Printing Technologies or teacher recommendation.
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

courses.description: This course will use the engineering design process of: Identify, Research, Imagine, Plan, Create, Test and Improve. This course focuses on problem solving and uses projects to solve those problems. Projects will include, but are not limited to, making CO2 cars, mouse trap cars, catapults, building classroom workspaces, website design, videography, chain reactions, cardboard escalator, among others. During this course the process is the most important thing, sometimes the builds will not work as planned, but the engineering design process will guide our learning and progress. This course will give you the basics you need to be able to convey your research, ideas and information in a way that can reach the online digital world. Students enrolled in this course can choose to earn either a Social Studies or Technology credit.
courses.fulfills_text: Students enrolled in this course can choose to earn either a Social Studies or Technology credit.
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Place-based course.

courses.description: In this course, students will team to produce a bi-weekly news broadcast program focused on Hartford High School. Students will learn how to use technology, including video cameras, microphones, and editing software to shoot and edit video stories, assemble scripts, and produce a news program. This course will prepare students for college and careers in a variety of professions by emphasizing 21st century skills involving communication, collaboration, creativity, and critical thinking. The goal by the end of the course is for students to be able to research multiple credible sources, use technology to revise and edit clips, report accurately and clearly to meet deadlines.
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Place-based course.

courses.description: This sports management course will have students diving into the world of event and game planning and management. Students will learn how to advertise, set up, and run a game or event. There will be a focus on creating digital and printable publications, in-game experiences including announcing and music, and data analysis of the event. Throughout this course we will learn from people who work in or have studied sports management and learn about post-high school opportunities in this field.
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Open to Grades 10-12 (Priority by age). Place-based course.

courses.description: Building on the foundations of Sports Management I, this course takes students deeper into the world of event and game planning, management, and execution. Students will take on leadership roles in organizing, advertising, and running sporting events while gaining hands-on experience in digital marketing, event logistics, and game-day operations.
courses.prerequisites: Sports Management 1 (scheduled simultaneously in the same classroom as Sports Management 1)
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Place-based course.

courses.description: Students will learn and apply French language skills to talk and write about themselves and to learn about people, places, and cultures in the Francophone world. By the end of the course, students will be able to communicate with memorized or familiar words and talk with others on a most basic level (the ACTFL novice-mid proficiency level). Students will also explore the benefits of learning a world language and practice language-learning strategies.
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

courses.description: Students will build on the skills they developed in French 1 as they listen, speak, read, and write about a variety of topics from the Francophone world, including current issues, sports, music, art, food, and geography. By the end of the course, students will be able to create simple sentences and questions (the ACTFL novice-high proficiency level).
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

courses.description: This course gives students additional tools to communicate in a variety of situations in French while continuing to explore the cultures and communities of the Francophone world. By the end of the course, students will be able to talk about familiar and researched topics and share opinions by creating simple sentences with more detail and by asking questions and follow-up questions (the ACTFL intermediate-low proficiency level).
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

courses.description: This course focuses on increasingly complex and nuanced aspects of the language and French-speaking cultures. We begin with a thorough review of grammar learned in previous courses. Students practice conversation, improve reading and listening skills, and build vocabulary. The course serves as a bridge to the AP French course offered in the spring, with much of the work designed to prepare students for AP French. It is highly recommended to take French 4 and AP French in the same school year. Students will take the ACTFL Assessment of Performance toward Proficiency in Languages (AAPPL) Exam at the end of the course; this is one path to earn the Seal of Biliteracy.
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall/Spring. Open to Grades 10-12 (Grade 9 requires instructor's permission).

courses.description: AP French Language and Culture continues the work students began in French 4. As students prepare to take the AP exam, they learn about a variety of French-speaking cultures and practice interpersonal, interpretive, and presentational communication. The course is comparable to a thirdyear college course. Learning experiences require students to integrate reading, writing, listening, and speaking in order to analyze and synthesize information from authentic French-language sources.
courses.prerequisites: It is highly recommended that French 4 be taken the semester immediately prior to taking AP French.
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Spring. Exam expectation: AP exam in May for a fee of approximately $90 (school covers the fee for students with additional financial need). Students enrolled in an AP course are expected to take the AP exam in the spring (fee); failure to take it changes the transcript identification to "Advanced" and the grade value from weighted to unweighted.

courses.description: Students will learn and apply Spanish language skills to talk and write about themselves and to learn about people, places, and cultures in the Spanish-speaking world. By the end of the course, students will be able to communicate with memorized or familiar words and talk with others on a most basic level (the ACTFL novice-mid proficiency level). Students will explore the benefits of learning a world language and practice language-learning strategies.
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

courses.description: Students will build on the skills they developed in Spanish 1 as they listen, speak, read, and write about a variety of topics from the Spanish-speaking world, including current issues, sports, music, art, food, and geography. By the end of the course, students will be able to create simple sentences and questions (the ACTFL novice-high proficiency level). Students will also explore the benefits of learning a world language and practice language-learning strategies.
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

courses.description: This intermediate course gives students additional tools to communicate in a variety of situations in Spanish while continuing to explore the cultures and communities of the Spanish-speaking world. Students will engage with a variety of audio-visual materials, including articles, shows, music and stories to develop their reading, listening, and interpretation skills in Spanish. By the end of the course, students will be able to talk about familiar topics and share opinions by creating simple sentences with more detail and by asking questions and follow-up questions (the ACTFL intermediate-low proficiency level).
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

courses.description: This course explores a variety of authentic cultural resources from the Spanish-speaking world and includes a thorough review of grammar. Students will engage with a variety of audio-visual materials, including articles, videos, music and stories to develop their reading, listening, and interpretation skills in Spanish. In addition, students will review and apply more advanced Spanish grammar concepts to enhance their writing and communication skills. They will write essays and opinion pieces as well as give oral presentations and have interpersonal conversations. Students will refine their fluency, critical thinking, and cultural awareness. By the end of the course, students will be able to talk and write about familiar and researched topics and share opinions by creating a series of connected sentences and by asking a variety of follow-up questions (the ACTFL intermediate-mid proficiency level). Students will take the ACTFL Assessment of Performance toward Proficiency in Languages (AAPPL) Exam at the end of the course; this is one path to earn the Seal of Biliteracy. This course can serve as a bridge to the AP Spanish course offered in the spring. This course is conducted entirely in Spanish.
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Open to Grades 10-12 (Grade 9 requires instructor's permission). Place-based course.

courses.description: This course explores a variety of cultures of the Spanish-speaking world and requires students to speak and write at length across various time frames (present, past and future). Students will engage with a variety of primary documents and audio-visual materials, including articles, videos, music, and stories to develop their reading, listening, and interpretation skills in Spanish. In addition, students will review and apply advanced Spanish grammar concepts to enhance their writing and communication skills. They will write 5-paragraph essays as well as give in-depth oral presentations and have lengthy interpersonal conversations. By the end of the course, students will be able to talk and write about a variety of topics and share opinions by creating a few short paragraphs and asking a variety of questions (the ACTFL intermediate-high proficiency level). Students will take the ACTFL Assessment of Performance toward Proficiency in Languages (AAPPL) Exam at the end of the course; this is one path to earn the Seal of Biliteracy. This course can serve as a bridge to the AP Spanish course offered in the spring or students may choose to take this course after AP Spanish. This course is conducted entirely in Spanish.
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Open to Grades 11-12 (Grade 10 requires instructor's permission).

courses.description: This course continues the work students begin in Spanish 4 and/or 5. As students prepare to take the AP exam, they will learn about a variety of Spanish-speaking cultures and demonstrate proficiency in interpersonal, interpretive, and presentational communication. In addition, students will have the opportunity to demonstrate understanding of the products, practices and perspectives of the target culture. The course is comparable to a third-year college course. Learning experiences require students to integrate reading, writing, listening, and speaking in order to analyze and synthesize information from authentic Spanish-language sources. By the end of the course, students will be able to write about a variety of topics and share opinions using paragraphs and exchange information and ideas in discussions. (the ACTFL advanced-low proficiency level). This course is conducted entirely in Spanish.
courses.prerequisites: Students MUST take Spanish 4 or Spanish 5 in the fall semester immediately prior to taking AP Spanish
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Spring Semester. Exam expectation: AP exam in May for a fee of approximately $90 (school covers the fee for students with additional financial need). Students enrolled in an AP course are expected to take the AP exam in the spring (fee); failure to take it changes the transcript identification to "Advanced" and the grade value from weighted to unweighted.

courses.description: Students will learn and apply German language skills to explore the visible and non-visible aspects of "culture" and encourage students to consider how products and practices differ in their own cultures and in a variety of cultures in the German-speaking world. Students will explore the reasons for learning a world language and discuss and practice language-learning strategies. Recognizing that students acquire language at different rates, students will target the ACTFL novice-mid proficiency level (talking about oneself using memorized or familiar words, expressing likes and dislikes, and talking with others on a most basic level).
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

courses.description: Students will build on the skills they developed in German 1 to explore intercultural perspectives as they listen, speak, read, and write in German. They will use the language to explore a variety of topics from the German-speaking world, including current issues, sports, music, art, food, and geography. Recognizing that students acquire language at different rates, students will target the ACTFL novice-high proficiency level (talking about oneself and familiar topics and asking original questions using simple sentences). Students will explore the reasons for learning a world language and practice language-learning strategies.
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

courses.description: This course expands upon work begun in previous levels and gives students additional tools to communicate in a variety of situations in German. We will continue to explore the cultures of the German-speaking world and begin something that interests them. Recognizing that students acquire language at different rates, students will target the ACTFL intermediate-low proficiency level (talking about familiar and researched topics and sharing opinions by creating simple sentences with more detail and asking appropriate follow-up questions). Students will explore the reasons for learning a world language and practice language-learning strategies.
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

courses.description: This course is an intermediate-level course that focuses on themes relevant to daily life in Germany, especially topics helpful to our exchange trip with our partner school in Germany. We look at German homes and towns, living with a host family, food, and school. We improve on ways to compare German culture to our own, describe how we're doing, and recount what has happened recently. We also focus on themes such as German history, architecture, sports, art, film, literature, Fascism, Communism, and Democracy; architecture and innovation; and other specific themes that interest the class. German 4 begins with a review of grammar and previously-learned vocabulary themes. Students build on reading and listening skills, as well as new vocabulary and expressions through various themes and topics covered throughout the semester. Students will take the ACTFL Assessment of Performance toward Proficiency in Languages (AAPPL) Exam at the end of the course; this is one path to earn the Seal of Biliteracy. The course can either stand alone or serve as a bridge to AP German. Our German program is designed to prepare students for two weeks of immersion in Germany living with families from our partner school. Students are expected to be enrolled in (or have completed) German 4 at the time of the trip during the years that this trip is offered.
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall.

courses.description: AP German Language and Culture continues the work students begin in German 4. As students prepare to take the AP exam, they learn about a variety of German-speaking cultures and practice interpersonal, interpretive, and presentational communication. The course is comparable to a third-year college course. Learning experiences require students to integrate reading, writing, listening, and speaking in order to analyze and synthesize information from authentic German-language sources.
courses.prerequisites: It is highly recommended that German 4 be taken the semester immediately prior to taking AP German.
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Spring. Exam expectation: AP exam in May for a fee of approximately $90 (school covers the fee for students with additional financial need). Students enrolled in an AP course are expected to take the AP exam in the spring (fee); failure to take it changes the transcript identification to "Advanced" and the grade value from weighted to unweighted.

courses.description: This course opportunity offers a hands-on introduction to the field of education with a focus on world language instruction. It is designed for students with strong interest in leadership, communication, and a world language. This experience supports growth in instructional skills, student mentorship, and classroom collaboration. Students will work with the teacher to create a course syllabus that meets the student’s learning objectives.
courses.prerequisites: Completion of French 3, German 3 or Spanish 4 or demonstrated proficiency AND teacher permission.
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

courses.description: Each and every Hartford student will have a different, unique, and personalized path through our school. Students will develop their Personalized Learning Plan (PLP) during Personalizing Pathways. Students will engage in activities designed to support their understanding of setting goals that are specific to their dreams and the creation of a living PLP that will allow them to drive their learning throughout their high school career.
courses.prerequisites: None (This course will be taken the opposite term of Wellness.)
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block / 1 Term, Fall / Spring. Required half-credit course for every grade 9 student (see graduation requirements).

courses.description: This course provides high school sophomores the opportunity to explore their post-high school goals. Students will reflect upon their strengths, interests, values, and goals by focusing on three key questions – Who am I? What are the habits of effective people? What will I do after high school? You will explore some of your post-high school options and learn skills to succeed in college, business, or the military. This course also provides students with an introduction to online learning, including an overview of CCVs portal environment. In addition, you will have Sophomore meetings with your school counselor, leading to next steps for your high school career and beyond. Other topics covered: time management, personal budgeting, and communication skills.
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall. Title includes "(CCV ICC)"; the description mentions an overview of the CCV portal environment; the catalog does not say whether college credit is earned.

courses.description: An opportunity to explore your future in higher education! You will spend the semester reflecting upon your strengths, interests, values, and goals by focusing on three key questions -- Who am I? What are the habits of effective people? What could college look like for me? This course opportunity offers a hands-on introduction to the field of education with a focus on world language instruction. It is designed for students with strong interest in leadership, communication, and a world language. This experience supports growth in instructional skills, student mentorship, and classroom collaboration. Students will work with the teacher to create a course syllabus that meets the student’s learning objectives. This class focuses on the skills necessary to apply for and succeed in higher education academic settings (including community, junior, and four-year colleges, trade and technical schools), and includes Junior meetings with your school counselor. Using the CCV platform in a hands-on environment, we will examine a variety of topics (driven by class interest), such as time management, interviewing, college searches and applications, personal budgeting and communication skills.
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Spring. Title includes "(CCV ICC)"; uses the CCV platform; the catalog does not say whether college credit is earned.

courses.description: This course embraces Student-Created Projects to expand learning experiences geared towards personal interests and goals. Students are encouraged to identify their passions and create their own authentic learning opportunities. Students will guide their own learning through connecting to and accessing resources to aid their endeavors. Teachers in this program serve as guides and resources for students to access experts in the community as much as possible; therefore, the experiences available are not limited to the walls or traditional schedule of Hartford High School. Students wishing to pursue this type of education must be able to work independently, collaborate with others and be willing to document and demonstrate their growth in Transferable Skills. They will show this growth using progress reflections, a final reflection and a public exhibition of their learning. Students enrolled in this course will receive an elective credit and may earn content-specific credit based on their project and collaboration with members of the appropriate department(s). This course may be repeated for multiple elective credits with the prerequisite of the instructor's permission. Some students may choose to participate in community-based learning. These learning opportunities may include: Volunteering, Internships, Job Shadows, or Work Experience. Students engaged in Student-Created Independent Projects with a focus on Community-based Learning will be required to reflect on their learning through the Transferable Skills standards as well as professional standards in accordance with their aligned profession or field. These students will partner with a mentor/supervisor who can assist them in developing their career-specific skills and will simply add these components to their final exhibition presentation. These students will receive an elective credit.
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Place-based course. May be repeated for multiple elective credits with the instructor's permission.

courses.description: This one-credit elective course is designed to help students venture outside of their comfort zones to improve their mental and physical well-being. Through the cultivation of a growth mindset, students will engage in various activities, discussions, and individualized projects. Participants will learn strategies for managing stress, building resilience, and fostering a mindset that embraces challenges for self-improvement. By exploring topics such as selfcare, emotional intelligence, and physical wellness, students will develop practical skills for maintaining a balanced and healthy lifestyle. Through student-centered experiential learning, this course prepares participants to navigate and embrace life's challenges with curiosity and confidence while equipping them with skills to thrive in areas of life deemed most important.
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Place-based course.

courses.description: WBL 1 (Employment Prep) is an educational program that combines classroom instruction with practical work experience that is directly related to student interests. The program’s mission is to enhance student knowledge by combining classroom learning with hands-on work experience. This includes opportunities such as interviews, job shadows, work experience, internships, apprenticeships, etc. Students will be required to reflect on their learning through Transferable Skill standards as well as professional standards in accordance with the aligned professional field. These students will partner with a mentor/supervisor who can assist them in developing their career-specific skills and will simply add these components to their portfolio for a final exhibition presentation. This class is Pass/Fail and students will receive an elective credit.
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Place-based course. Pass/Fail; elective credit.

courses.description: WBL2 (Work Study) is a course where students who are currently employed will be fully immersed in a work-based educational experience. Students will collaborate and create educational goals with an employer and the Work Based Learning Coordinator to allow them to work four days a week while learning skills in their current occupation to prepare them for post secondary life. Students will create a plan on what topics, skills, and goals that will be needed for the career focused experience and will meet with the Work Based Learning coordinator weekly for check in and discuss Transferable skills. They will participate in all Work Based Learning scheduled trips and activities, such as business panels and mock interviews and will gather evidence of their learning from the course and create a product for a final exhibition presentation. This class is Pass/Fail and students will receive an elective credit.
courses.prerequisites: Demonstrated skills as reflected in WBL-Employment Prep or school counselor recommendation
courses.notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Place-based course. Pass/Fail; elective credit.

courses.description: Edmentum is an online learning platform that provides the opportunity for students to learn anywhere they have access to Wi-Fi and a computer at any time. Students can enroll in these online courses (referred to as QUEST classes) if (1) the course does not exist in name or content in the Hartford High School Program of Studies or (2) the student has failed the equivalent course and in doing so exhausted teachers who teach the course or (3) the student is unable to schedule a course that exists as a link in a sequence of courses that will prohibit the student from attaining the highest level possible in the sequence or (4) the student's counselor and/or case manager identifies that the online version of the course better serves the student's individual learning needs.
courses.notes: program; individual online course titles are not listed in the catalog. Online courses are referred to as QUEST classes.

courses.description: Hartford High School recognizes that there can be occasions when a student’s educational interests are best served by engaging in an independent study with a teacher in the appropriate content area. The student will identify appropriate proficiency-based standards, including the transferable skills, which they will work toward achieving through their Student-Created Independent Project experience. Students will work closely with a sponsoring professional/teacher in the content area appropriate for their project. The individually developed project will be supported through regular contact with a high school teacher and will result in an exhibition or display of learning as a culminating presentation.
courses.notes: program

courses.department: Guidelines for Obtaining Credit for Alternative Coursework
courses.description: This represents an excellent opportunity to get a head start on accruing college credits, as well as obtaining credit applicable to high school graduation. In order to participate in a dual enrollment course students need to complete the dual enrollment process with their school counselor.
courses.prerequisites: Students must identify their desire to take a Dual Enrollment course through their Personalized Learning Plan - PLP.
courses.notes: program. Catalog: two courses may be taken and paid for by the state of Vermont/local district; students may take courses beginning the summer of their sophomore year until graduation; the course must be at a participating Vermont college; the college grade appears on the HHS transcript. Elsewhere the catalog says dual enrollment is for juniors and seniors (p.4) and a PLP must be in place for 11th/12th graders (p.5). A full-term three- or four-credit college course equals one one-credit, semester-long high school course (p.8).

courses.course_name: Dartmouth College Courses (Special Community Student Program)
courses.department: Guidelines for Obtaining Credit for Alternative Coursework
courses.description: This unique opportunity is provided through the Special Community Student Program and is for advanced students who want to take one or more classes at Dartmouth College while earning college credit in high school. Students interested in learning more about this program should contact their high school counselor.
courses.prerequisites: Second semester juniors and all seniors who meet the eligibility requirements
courses.notes: program. Students may take as many as 4 courses at Dartmouth College; HHS transcript shows "P" (Pass) or "F" (Fail); the "P" is not calculated into the GPA.

courses.course_code: 1623 (Autobody, Motorsports & Customs 1) / 1624 (Autobody, Motorsports & Customs / Math 2) / 1625 (Autobody, Motorsports & Cust. / Science 2)
courses.description: Students will be introduced to the fields of Autobody, Motorsports and Customs (AMC). Students in AMC get to use top-of-the-line equipment and technology like the DeVilbiss semi-downdraft paint booth, PPG Aquabase paint mixing system, and commercial quality vinyl cutting machine. The curriculum focuses on mechanics, body repair and replacement, sanding, masking, painting, and use and care of high tech spray equipment. Students gain hands-on experience as they prepare for career opportunities in autobody repair, metal fabrication, painting, graphics, motorsports, restoration and customization of vehicles, and more, depending on student interests. With permission from the instructor, students may work on “live jobs'' brought in by the local community. This program is ASE Education Foundation certified. After completing this program, students have had success entering directly into the workforce or going on to post-secondary education.
courses.fulfills_text: Embedded Credits: 1 Math credit or 1 Science credit
courses.notes: program (two-year sequence; Level 1 / Level 2). General HACTC rules: eligible incoming juniors and seniors (sophomores may register for STEM or Information Technology courses); programs occupy 1 1/2 blocks daily; separate HACTC application required; upon completing both levels a student receives 5 elective credits in the career program and 1 embedded credit. Leadership Club: Automotive and Collision Enthusiasts Club (ACE). Industry Certifications: Non-structural Analysis and Damage Repair ASE entry level certification test; Maintenance and Light Repair ASE entry level certification; Painting and Refinishing ASE entry level certification; S/P2 online safety training; and WorkKeys National Career Readiness Certification (NCRC).

courses.description: Automotive Technology trains and prepares students to become successful automotive technicians, for jobs in related fields or post-secondary education. Students are trained both in the classroom and on HACTC shop vehicles. Our emphasis is on safe, honest, ethical and professional work habits and skills. We follow a best practices approach to automotive repair. Units are aligned with the National Institute of Automotive Service Excellence (ASE), and students have the opportunity to take an ASE exam and earn an entry-level Industry Recognized Credential (IRC) at the conclusion of each unit. Students will utilize individual skills as well as team based learning to become proficient at problem solving and time management. Qualified Level 2 students will have the opportunity for a Cooperative Education placement with local automotive employers.
courses.fulfills_text: Embedded Credit: 1 Science credit
courses.notes: program (two-year sequence; Level 1 / Level 2). General HACTC rules: eligible incoming juniors and seniors (sophomores may register for STEM or Information Technology courses); programs occupy 1 1/2 blocks daily; separate HACTC application required; upon completing both levels a student receives 5 elective credits in the career program and 1 embedded credit. Leadership Club: Automotive and Collision Enthusiasts Club (ACE). College Course Option: None at this time. Industry Certifications: 9 ASE Entry Level Certifications; Lift it Right Certification; WorkKeys National Career Readiness Certification (NCRC).

courses.description: Students get hands-on access in the professional trades while they work to build a house from the ground up. This two-year program guides students through building a brand new energy-efficient house from beginning to end. This is a real world/life experience for students to safely practice and learn work ethic and a new skill set. During this process, students will learn everything from beginning tool safety, skill techniques, and blueprint reading through residential plumbing and electrical. Students also have the chance to work with subcontractors who are hired to work at the house throughout the building process. Safety is our goal 100% of the time. Students are also exposed to real world experiences on field trips, job shadowing and Cooperative Education learning experiences. Upon program completion, students are qualified to walk into most entry-level positions within the Building Trades arena, pursue apprenticeships, or further their education.
courses.fulfills_text: Embedded Credit: 1 Math credit
courses.notes: program (two-year sequence; Level 1 / Level 2). General HACTC rules: eligible incoming juniors and seniors (sophomores may register for STEM or Information Technology courses); programs occupy 1 1/2 blocks daily; separate HACTC application required; upon completing both levels a student receives 5 elective credits in the career program and 1 embedded credit. Leadership Club: None at this time. College Course Option: None at this time. Industry Certifications: NCCER Core and Carpentry Modules; OSHA-10; and WorkKeys National Career Readiness Certification (NCRC).

courses.description: Business, Entrepreneurship and Marketing (BEM) students are people who want to develop their business and communication skills for use in a variety of contexts. This program leads students through all aspects of the business world, from accounting and personal finance to marketing and professional communications. Students develop their own sharp business skills through individual and group projects, Cooperative Education placements, and guest lectures from industry professionals. BEM students have the opportunity to participate in Future Business Leaders of America (FBLA), earn up to 12 college credits and four industry recognized certifications, and build a professional business and communications portfolio.
courses.fulfills_text: Embedded Credit: 1 English credit
courses.notes: program (two-year sequence; Level 1 / Level 2). General HACTC rules: eligible incoming juniors and seniors (sophomores may register for STEM or Information Technology courses); programs occupy 1 1/2 blocks daily; separate HACTC application required; upon completing both levels a student receives 5 elective credits in the career program and 1 embedded credit. Leadership Club: Future Business Leaders of America (FBLA). College Course Options: River Valley Community College - Introduction to Business (3 credits); Small Business Management (3 credits); Accounting 1 (3 credits); and Personal Financial Management (3 credits). Industry Certifications: CareerSafe OSHA-10 Certification; Ergonomics; Quickbooks Online Pro Advisor; WorkKeys National Career Readiness Certification (NCRC).

courses.course_name: Career & Technology Exploration Program (Sophomore Students Only)
courses.description: CTE is a unique program to the HACTC, open only to high school sophomores. This classroom model is meant to offer a unique and holistic learning experience. Students are referred for admission to the CTE program by their school counselor. Small-group and one-on-one instruction are at the heart of helping Career Technology Exploration (CTE) students reconnect to their own educational experience. The more individualized, hands-on and supported instruction is vital in helping students find success in school and improving their overall educational experience. The CTE program helps students earn traditional high school credits while providing early exposure to Career and Technical Education. Students cycle back and forth between time in the CTE classroom and placements in the HACTC technical programs, giving students an up close and hands-on introduction to HACTC opportunities. While in their own classroom, CTE students focus on high school math, English, and art credits. Upon successful completion of the CTE program, students will have the opportunity to apply to an HACTC program for their junior year.
courses.fulfills_text: Embedded Credits: 1 Math credit, 1 English credit, and 1 Fine Art credit
courses.notes: program. Open only to high school sophomores; students are referred for admission by their school counselor.

courses.description: The HACTC Cosmetology Program provides students the skills and experiences they need to become licensed Cosmetologists. Completing 1,000 hours of study, students will master skills in hair design, nail and skincare, personal appearance, communication, and business management. Students learn and put into practice these skills through demonstrations on mannequins and by working with fellow students and live clients in a salon setting. Students have the opportunity to earn their Cosmetology licensure in the State of Vermont by successfully completing this rigorous college-level program.
courses.fulfills_text: Embedded Credits: 1 Science credit
courses.notes: program (two-year sequence; Level 1 / Level 2). General HACTC rules: eligible incoming juniors and seniors (sophomores may register for STEM or Information Technology courses); programs occupy 1 1/2 blocks daily; separate HACTC application required; upon completing both levels a student receives 5 elective credits in the career program and 1 embedded credit. Leadership Club: Future Business Leaders of America (FBLA). Industry Certifications: Vermont Cosmetology Licensure, S/P2 Cosmetology Safety and Sanitation Certification; Barbicide Certification; Conover Workplace Readiness; Lucacide/Sol Certification; Pivot Point International Units of Measurement, and WorkKeys National Career Readiness Certification (NCRC). Program involves 1,000 hours of study.

courses.description: The Culinary Arts program is a fast-paced learning environment grounded in food science, safety, sanitation, customer service and the basic principles of cooking. With our cafe-style restaurant named The Getaway, students are exposed to a practical application of skills in a dynamic, rigorous curriculum. Students will demonstrate a basic knowledge of the food service industry, including: organizational flow, Hazard Analysis Critical Control Point (HACCP), sanitation practices, personal hygiene, equipment and utensil identification and use, basic first aid, nutrition, customer service, basic food and bakeshop techniques, as well as storage, handling of food and math applications.
courses.fulfills_text: Embedded Credit: 1 Science credit
courses.notes: program (two-year sequence; Level 1 / Level 2). General HACTC rules: eligible incoming juniors and seniors (sophomores may register for STEM or Information Technology courses); programs occupy 1 1/2 blocks daily; separate HACTC application required; upon completing both levels a student receives 5 elective credits in the career program and 1 embedded credit. Leadership Club: Hospitality Club. College Course Option: Lakes Region Community College - Culinary Fundamentals (3 credits); Sanitation and Safety (3 credits); and Bakery Production (3 credits). Industry Certifications: American Culinary Federation Secondary Graduate Certification; ServSafe Manager; and WorkKeys National Career Readiness Certification (NCRC).

courses.description: The Design and Illustration and Media Arts (DIMA) program at the HACTC is full of creative thinkers. Students in both levels work through projects that introduce them to technical skills in this exciting industry while still exploring their personal interests through self-directed projects. Students use industry standard Mac platform software with the most up-to-date Adobe hardware. Students work through projects that introduce them to many different aspects of digital illustration, digital video production, digital photography, 2-D animation, and motion graphics. Students also accept “live jobs” from the public sector and must learn how to create professional quality work products, follow real-world timelines and work with clients. Students will prepare themselves for endeavors after high school by creating a professional online portfolio, resume and cover letter that they can use for post secondary education or the workforce.
courses.fulfills_text: Embedded Credits: 1 Fine Art credit
courses.notes: program (two-year sequence; Level 1 / Level 2). General HACTC rules: eligible incoming juniors and seniors (sophomores may register for STEM or Information Technology courses); programs occupy 1 1/2 blocks daily; separate HACTC application required; upon completing both levels a student receives 5 elective credits in the career program and 1 embedded credit. Leadership Club: Future Business Leaders of America (FBLA). College Course Option: Lakes Region Community College - Introduction to Digital Photography (3 credits); Digital Illustration (3 credits); Foundations of Design (3 credits); and Design Software Essentials (3 credits). Industry Certifications: Adobe Photoshop CC; Adobe Illustrator CC; and WorkKeys National Career Readiness Certification (NCRC) Vermont Arts Portifolio.

courses.description: Are you interested in helping people, working in healthcare, and making a difference in your community? Health and Human Sciences is a fast-paced, hands-on program where students will learn skills, explore careers and earn both a license and certification before graduating high school. Students will have the opportunity to earn their Licensed Nursing Assistant (LNA) license and Phlebotomy certification. Students will practice skills in the classroom as both patient and provider, and in healthcare settings. This means students need to be comfortable being touched by peers, as well as using real needles to draw blood. Students may also earn college credits in each year of the program, and complete Cooperative Education rotations in various health care settings.
courses.fulfills_text: Embedded Credit: 1 Science credit
courses.notes: program (two-year sequence; Level 1 / Level 2). General HACTC rules: eligible incoming juniors and seniors (sophomores may register for STEM or Information Technology courses); programs occupy 1 1/2 blocks daily; separate HACTC application required; upon completing both levels a student receives 5 elective credits in the career program and 1 embedded credit. Leadership Club: Future Health Professionals (HOSA). College Course Option: River Valley Community College - Introduction to Psychology (3 credits); and Supportive Communication Skills (3 credits). Industry Certifications: Licensed Nursing Assistant (LNA); Certified Phlebotomy Technician (CPT); Basic Life Support (BLS) for Healthcare Providers: CPR and AED; First Aid; Bloodborne Pathogens; Stop the Bleed Certification and WorkKeys National Career Readiness Certification (NCRC).

courses.description: This course exposes students to a wide range of topics designed to instill general fabrication skills combined with technical subjects. The course prepares students for a wide range of occupations such as welding, electrical, machining, and mechanical trades. Students routinely use math and science skills and interact with STEM, Automotive Technology, Natural Resources and Autobody, Motorsports and Customs programs while working on projects. Students are prepared for a career or post-secondary education with technical skills, a positive attitude and a strong work ethic.
courses.fulfills_text: Embedded Credits: 1 Science credit
courses.notes: program (two-year sequence; Level 1 / Level 2). General HACTC rules: eligible incoming juniors and seniors (sophomores may register for STEM or Information Technology courses); programs occupy 1 1/2 blocks daily; separate HACTC application required; upon completing both levels a student receives 5 elective credits in the career program and 1 embedded credit. Industry Certifications: S/P2 Environmental Safety Training Certification; American Welding Society 1G Structural Steel Certification; and WorkKeys National Career Readiness Certification (NCRC).

courses.course_name: Information Technology (One-year course in the P.M.)
courses.description: The Information Technology program is designed for students who are interested in exploring a career in the growing tech industry. Over the course of the year, students will gain valuable hands-on experience in computer repair, user support, and networking and have the opportunity to obtain two valuable industry certifications as well as six college credits. Students will also explore careers across the field and practice the skills necessary to earn a job in this growing sector. Lastly, students will spend some time each week discussing topics of interest like cybersecurity, big data, artificial intelligence and the impact these technologies have on our modern world.
courses.fulfills_text: Yearlong Credits: 1 Technology credit, 0.5 English credit, 1.5 elective credits
courses.notes: program (one-year course). College Course Options: Community College of Vermont - Concepts of PC Hardware (3 credits) and Desktop Operating Systems (3 credits). Industry Certifications: COMPTIA A+; and WorkKeys National Career Readiness Certification (NCRC). Sophomores may register for STEM or Information Technology courses.

courses.course_name: Software Engineering (One-year course in the A.M.)
courses.description: The Software Engineering Program will give students the foundational skills necessary to pursue a career in software development, or dev ops. Students will be given a thorough introduction to Python, one of the world’s most popular programming languages, and learn valuable software development skills along the way. At the end of the year students undertake a substantial project where they will have the opportunity to learn a new technology or framework, taking an idea from requirements to implementation.
courses.fulfills_text: Yearlong Credits: 1 Technology credit, 0.5 Math credit, 1.5 elective credits
courses.notes: program (one-year course). College Course Option: River Valley Community College - Introduction to Python (4 credits). Industry Certifications: WorkKeys National Career Readiness Certification (NCRC). Catalog does not say whether sophomores may enroll (it names STEM and Information Technology courses for sophomores).

courses.description: The Natural Resources program is a practical application of skills in a hands-on learning environment. Students will discover and explore the many careers that Natural Resources has to offer through field experiences, community projects, and exposure to experts in various fields. Students will be prepared for a career or further education with technical skills, a positive attitude and a strong work ethic. Qualified Level two students will have the opportunity for Cooperative Education placements with local businesses.
courses.fulfills_text: Embedded Credits: 1 Science credit
courses.notes: program (two-year sequence; Level 1 / Level 2). General HACTC rules: eligible incoming juniors and seniors (sophomores may register for STEM or Information Technology courses); programs occupy 1 1/2 blocks daily; separate HACTC application required; upon completing both levels a student receives 5 elective credits in the career program and 1 embedded credit. Leadership Club: FFA. College Course Option: None at this time. Industry Certifications: Game of Logging 1 and 2 (for Level 1 students); Game of Logging 3 and 4 (for Level 2 students); LEAP Certification and WorkKeys National Career Readiness Certification (NCRC).

courses.course_name: Introduction to Engineering Design (STEM) (One-year course in the P.M.)
courses.description: Using the Project Lead the Way curriculum, Introduction to Engineering Design (IED) students are introduced to the engineering design process. This program focuses on applying math, science, and engineering standards to identify and design solutions to a variety of real problems. Students will work both individually and in collaborative teams to develop and document design solutions using engineering notebooks, 2D and 3D modeling software, a laser engraver, a 3D printer, and a CNC router, as well as a host of traditional tools. Students develop skills in problem solving, manufacturing, research and design process documentation and presentation. IED is a one-year long course offered in the P.M.
courses.prerequisites: Concurrently enrolled in Algebra 1 or have completed it with a C- or better
courses.fulfills_text: Year-Long Credits: 1 Engineering credit, 1 Technology credit, 1 Physical Science credit
courses.notes: program (one-year course). College Course Option: St. Cloud State University - Introduction to Engineering Design (3 credits). Industry Certifications: WorkKeys National Career Readiness Certification (NCRC). Sophomores may register for STEM courses.

courses.course_name: Principles of Engineering/Physics (STEM) (One-year course in the A.M.)
courses.description: While using the Project Lead the Way curriculum, Principles of Engineering (POE) students work through problems that engage and challenge, while exploring a broad range of physics and engineering topics, including mechanical and electrical design, developing sustainability, the strength of structures and materials (civil engineering), and the application of robotics using computer programming in Python. Students continue to refine skills in problem solving, manufacturing, research, and design, while learning strategies for design process documentation, collaboration, and presentation. POE is a one-year long course offered in the A.M.
courses.prerequisites: Concurrently enrolled in Algebra 2 or have completed it with a C- or better
courses.fulfills_text: High School Credit Option: 1 credit Physics, 1 credit Engineering, 1 credit Technology
courses.notes: program (one-year course). College Course Option: St. Cloud State University - Principles of Engineering (3 credits). Industry Certification: WorkKeys National Career Readiness Certification (NCRC). Sophomores may register for STEM courses.
